# Attribution Report: Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks

## Executive assessment

The available evidence supports the conclusion that **Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks were not independent Romanian or American hacktivist personas, but fronts used in a GRU-controlled influence and disclosure operation**. The strongest attribution chain is presented in the July 2018 U.S. Department of Justice indictment, which alleges that officers of GRU Units 26165 and 74455 hacked Democratic campaign and party networks, created and operated the two personas, used overlapping infrastructure and financing, and transferred stolen material to a separate publication organization. CrowdStrike’s incident-response account independently describes the DNC intrusion, identifies the relevant malware and adversary tradecraft, and places X-Agent and X-Tunnel activity within the same operational environment later described in the indictment.

This conclusion should be stated with appropriate legal and evidentiary qualifications. The indictment contains **criminal allegations**, not adjudicated findings of guilt. CrowdStrike’s account is an **incident-response and threat-intelligence assessment produced by a private company**, although the supplied material also reports that its conclusions were supported by U.S. intelligence and congressional reviews. The evidence nevertheless forms a coherent attribution chain: intrusion activity, malware, operator behavior, infrastructure, cryptocurrency funding, persona creation, document dissemination, and coordination with an external publication organization. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election); [S2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

## Sources and evidentiary status

| Source ID | Source | Type | Evidentiary status |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | U.S. Department of Justice, July 13, 2018 indictment | Federal charging document | Allegations made by a grand jury and Special Counsel; not a conviction |
| S2 | CrowdStrike, “Bears in the Midst: Intrusion Into the Democratic National Committee” and later updates | Private incident-response and threat-intelligence account | Corporate assessment, technical observations, and later explanations of its investigative process |

The sources are complementary. S1 provides the most detailed public narrative connecting named GRU officers, units, online personas, infrastructure, cryptocurrency payments, and releases. S2 supplies contemporaneous technical context concerning the DNC intrusion, including the identification of “COZY BEAR” and “FANCY BEAR,” the use of X-Agent and X-Tunnel, and the distinction between the two intrusion operations observed on the DNC network. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election); [S2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

## The persona narrative

### DCLeaks

According to the indictment, GRU-linked operators registered the dcleaks.com domain on or about April 19, 2016, more than a month before the first public releases. The domain was registered through an anonymization service and paid for with cryptocurrency. The indictment further alleges that the same operational email account used to support DCLeaks was also associated with the URL-shortening account “john356gh,” which was used in spearphishing directed at the Clinton campaign chairman and other campaign-related individuals. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The site was launched on or about June 8, 2016. The indictment alleges that it released emails stolen from Clinton campaign affiliates and other victims, while falsely claiming to have been created by “American hacktivists.” It also alleges that GRU operators created and managed related social-media accounts, including a Facebook page using the fictitious name “Alice Donovan,” accounts using the names “Jason Scott” and “Richard Gingrey,” and the Twitter account @dcleaks_. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The attribution significance is not merely that DCLeaks published stolen material. The indictment alleges that the persona was constructed **before publication**, financed through the same cryptocurrency ecosystem used for hacking infrastructure, and administered through computers associated with GRU Unit 74455. This is consistent with a planned influence operation rather than an opportunistic leak outlet. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

### Guccifer 2.0

The indictment alleges that Guccifer 2.0 was created on or about June 14, 2016, after the DNC publicly announced that Russian government actors had compromised its network. The persona allegedly claimed to be a lone Romanian hacker in order to undermine the Russian-attribution explanation. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The indictment describes an unusually specific operational link. On June 15, 2016, operators allegedly logged into a Moscow-based server used and managed by Unit 74455 and searched for English words and phrases that appeared shortly afterward in Guccifer 2.0’s first blog post. The searched phrases included “worldwide known,” “think twice about,” “company’s competence,” “some hundreds of sheets,” “dcleaks,” and “illuminati.” The first Guccifer 2.0 post used those expressions in presenting the supposed “lone hacker” narrative. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

This sequence is significant because it links the persona’s public communications to activity on infrastructure allegedly controlled by Unit 74455 and to a same-day search history. Standing alone, linguistic overlap would not establish attribution. Combined with the alleged server access, subsequent infrastructure overlap, and transfer of stolen documents, it materially strengthens the case that Guccifer 2.0 was operated by the same GRU-linked campaign.

## Technical and infrastructure links

### X-Agent and X-Tunnel

CrowdStrike reported identifying two separate adversaries on the DNC network: COZY BEAR and FANCY BEAR. It associated FANCY BEAR with X-Agent and X-Tunnel, describing X-Agent as capable of remote command execution, file transmission, and keylogging, and X-Tunnel as a tool for network tunneling and remote-command activity. ([S2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

The indictment independently alleges that GRU Unit 26165 was responsible for hacking the DCCC and DNC and for targeting individuals affiliated with the Clinton campaign. It identifies Sergey Morgachev as supervising malware development and management, Nikolay Kozachek as developing and monitoring X-Agent, Pavel Yershov as assisting with testing and customization, and Artem Malyshev as monitoring X-Agent implants. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The two sources therefore converge on the same operational tools and activity:

| Operational element | S1 indictment | S2 CrowdStrike account |
|---|---|---|
| X-Agent | Allegedly implanted on DCCC and DNC computers for monitoring, keylogging, screenshots, and persistence | Described as FANCY BEAR malware used for command execution, file transmission, and keylogging |
| X-Tunnel | Allegedly used to move stolen documents through encrypted channels | Described as a tunneling tool capable of facilitating connections and remote commands |
| GRU association | Attributes the activity to Units 26165 and 74455 | Assesses FANCY BEAR as closely linked to Russian military intelligence |
| DNC intrusion | Allegedly began in April 2016 for the Unit 26165 operation | Identifies a separate FANCY BEAR breach in April 2016 |

The technical overlap does not by itself prove that every person associated with the personas personally operated every malware component. It does, however, support an organizational attribution in which the personas, malware, and disclosure activity were components of a common GRU-linked operation. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election); [S2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

### Shared infrastructure and financing

The indictment alleges that Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks used overlapping infrastructure and financing. Between March 14 and April 28, 2016, operators allegedly used the same pool of bitcoin funds to purchase a VPN account and lease a Malaysian server. The Malaysian server was later used to host dcleaks.com, while the VPN was allegedly used to access the @Guccifer_2 Twitter account. The indictment also alleges that the VPN account was opened from a server used to register malicious domains associated with the DCCC and DNC intrusions. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

This is one of the strongest links in the attribution chain because it connects:

1. a communications or concealment service;
2. the DCLeaks website;
3. the Guccifer 2.0 social-media account; and
4. domains allegedly used in the underlying intrusion.

The indictment further alleges that more than $95,000 in cryptocurrency transactions were used to purchase servers, register domains, and maintain hacking infrastructure. It describes fictitious names, false addresses, hundreds of email accounts, bitcoin mining, peer-to-peer exchanges, and layered transactions intended to obscure the operators’ identities and connection to Russia. These allegations explain how the operators could maintain ostensibly independent personas while controlling their infrastructure centrally. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

## The release chain

The indictment alleges that Guccifer 2.0 transferred stolen materials to “Organization 1,” which is not named in the charging document. The alleged communications show the organization requesting new DNC material, discussing timing before the Democratic National Convention, and emphasizing the expected political impact of Hillary Clinton-related disclosures. The operators allegedly sent an encrypted file containing instructions for accessing an archive of stolen DNC documents. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

On July 22, 2016, Organization 1 allegedly released more than 20,000 emails and documents stolen from the DNC. The indictment states that the release occurred approximately three days before the Democratic National Convention. It later alleges that, beginning October 7, 2016, Organization 1 released approximately 33 tranches of material stolen from the Clinton campaign chairman, totaling more than 50,000 documents. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The release chain thus appears to have had several layers:

- **Unit 26165:** alleged intrusion, credential theft, malware deployment, and data theft;
- **Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks:** alleged cover identities and public-facing distribution channels;
- **Unit 74455:** alleged administration of infrastructure, promotion of releases, and social-media activity;
- **Organization 1:** alleged high-impact publication of selected stolen material.

The evidence supports the assessment that the personas were designed not only to publish material, but also to create distance between the Russian military-intelligence operators and the final disclosures. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

## Relationship between incident-response evidence and the indictment

CrowdStrike’s initial June 2016 account identified COZY BEAR and FANCY BEAR as separate adversaries on the DNC network and assessed FANCY BEAR as consistent with Russian military-intelligence activity. It also reported that the FANCY BEAR intrusion involved X-Agent, X-Tunnel, spearphishing, command execution, keylogging, and anti-forensic activity. ([S2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

The later indictment gives those technical observations a specific organizational framework: Unit 26165, Unit 74455, named officers, domains, servers, cryptocurrency transactions, persona management, and publication coordination. This does not mean the indictment simply proves every detail in CrowdStrike’s original account. Rather, the two sources provide mutually reinforcing layers:

- CrowdStrike supplies technical incident-response observations and actor assessments.
- The indictment supplies a prosecutorial narrative connecting the technical activity to named GRU units and individuals.
- The indictment’s alleged infrastructure and financing links connect the intrusion phase to the persona and release phase.

CrowdStrike also states that it did not directly investigate John Podesta’s email leaks and did not physically take possession of DNC servers; it describes its work as forensic imaging, analysis, and remediation. That limitation should be preserved. The public evidence does not justify saying that CrowdStrike itself observed every later transfer or publication event in real time. ([S2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

## Contradictions and limitations

The apparent contradiction is between the personas’ public claims and the attribution evidence. Guccifer 2.0 allegedly claimed to be a lone Romanian hacker, while DCLeaks allegedly claimed to be an American hacktivist collective. The indictment characterizes both claims as false cover stories. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

A second limitation concerns the distinction between direct and circumstantial evidence. CrowdStrike’s later explanation states that it had indicators and circumstantial evidence of data exfiltration rather than a network sensor recording the theft in real time. The indictment, however, alleges specific theft mechanisms, including compressed archives, X-Tunnel transfers, cloud snapshots, and stolen credentials. These are different evidentiary descriptions, not necessarily irreconcilable accounts. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election); [S2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

A final limitation is legal status. No supplied source establishes that the indicted defendants were tried and convicted. The proper formulation is therefore that the indictment **alleges** the conduct and that the combined technical and documentary evidence **supports** the attribution assessment.

## Conclusion

On the supplied evidence, the Guccifer 2.0/DCLeaks narrative is best resolved as a **fabricated-front theory rather than an authentic independent-hacker account**. The attribution is supported by five connected elements: the GRU-linked intrusion into DNC and DCCC systems; use of X-Agent and X-Tunnel; shared servers, VPNs, domains, and cryptocurrency funding; alleged access to Unit 74455 infrastructure during the creation of Guccifer 2.0; and the coordinated transfer and timed release of stolen documents.

The most defensible conclusion is not that every public detail has been independently proven beyond dispute, nor that the indictment is equivalent to a conviction. It is that the evidence establishes a highly coherent operational relationship between the personas and GRU-controlled election-interference activity, and that the “lone Romanian hacker” and “American hacktivist” explanations are inconsistent with the infrastructure, malware, financing, and release-chain evidence described in the two sources.
